newsitem.title: USA: U.S. livestock industry cautiously eyes cloning.
newsitem.headline: U.S. livestock industry cautiously eyes cloning.

text.p: Reaction from the U.S. livestock industry to news of the first successful cloning of a farm animal was mostly muted as even biotechnology promoters seemed cautious about the breakthrough.
Producing beef steaks or pork chops that are similar in taste and appearance could possibly be solved by cloning cattle and pigs, some livestock specialists said.
"In my opinion it could be implemented in a very short time," Roger McCaw, a beef specialist at North Carolina State University extension, said on Monday.
"From a technical standpoint, I would expect it within three years."
Livestock specialists at Purdue University said it would take a few years for cloning to become a commercial tool.
Expected legal challenges and protest from consumer groups would likely slow introduction, as would government regulation of cloning, said Larry Nelson, a Purdue animal scientist.
"I'm sure it's going to be maybe a few years down the road...before it is utilised in the livestock community," he said. "It also is going to be highly regulated by the government entities."

Scottish researcher Ian Wilmut, working with Edinburgh biotechnology company PPL Therapeutics , cloned a sheep using an embryo cell and a cell from another sheep's mammary gland. PPL has filed a patent claim on the technology.

Successful cloning of the sheep, which attracted worldwide media coverage at the weekend, had "occurred sooner than most expected," the BioTechnology Industry Organization, a Washington, D.C.,-based group, said in a statement.
"The biotechnology industry exists to use genetic information to cure disease and improve agriculture," it said.

"We opposed human cloning when it was a theory. Now that it may be possible, we urge that it be prohibited by law," said the group, which represents about 700 biotechnology companies, academic institutions and other research centers.
Biotechnology already has a firm foothold and growing presence in U.S. agriculture including production of milk, corn, soybeans, cotton and corn.

North Carolina State's McCaw said the beef and dairy industries would likely be first to benefit from cloning since both already have extensive genetic and performance databases that would help identify prime candidates for cloning.
Many in the livestock industry remained reserved in assessing the impact of the successful cloning.

The National Cattlemen's Beef Association said in a statement it has an official policy supporting biotechnology and genetic engineering that improve production efficiency and enhance consumer products. But it omitted any reference specifically to support of cloning.

Dairy Management Inc, a marketing group for U.S. dairy farmers, said it supports science that benefits dairy farmers. But on the issue of cloning, "it is premature to make any assumptions at this time," the group said.
